Chapter 2: The Birth of Aggressive Pharmaceutical Marketing
In medicine, trust really is everything. You trust your doctor, your doctor trusts science, and deep down, we all hope the system is looking out for us, right?
But what if that trust could actually be turned into a tool... for making money?
The Sackler brothers—especially Arthur—spotted something early on. The real power in medicine wasn’t just about discovering new drugs. It was about getting people to use them. Arthur changed the game in medical advertising across America. He realized doctors are the gatekeepers. If you could win them over, you could shape the whole market.
This was a totally new way of thinking. Instead of waiting for doctors to come looking for new treatments, Arthur brought those treatments right to their doorstep. Picture glossy ads, sponsored medical journals, and big, impressive conferences. He even pioneered direct mail campaigns, sending info about new drugs straight to doctors’ offices. The message? This medicine is safe, effective, and your patients need it.
One of the first big examples? The promotion of Valium. If you’ve ever heard of it, you know Valium became one of the most prescribed drugs in history. The campaign behind it was relentless. Doctors were told it could help with everything—anxiety, muscle spasms—you name it. Risks were brushed aside, benefits pumped up. And sales? They soared. The whole pharmaceutical industry started to pay attention.
The massive success of Valium set the tone for what came next. The Sacklers realized that, with the right message, you could sell just about any drug. They built close relationships with influential doctors, funded research that made their products look good, and made sure any bad news... well, it just didn’t get much attention.
This approach changed the entire industry. Suddenly, it was hard to tell where education ended and advertising began. Most doctors didn’t even notice the shift. They trusted the information they received, never realizing it was often shaped by the very companies selling the drugs.
As Purdue Frederick grew, the Sacklers started thinking even bigger. What if they could launch a product that would completely transform the company—and their fortunes? They set their sights on pain. Pain touches millions of lives, but for years, it hadn’t gotten much attention from doctors. The Sacklers believed that if they could find a better way to treat pain, they could change the world—and make a fortune along the way.
By then, the groundwork was done. The marketing tools were all in place. All they needed now was the right drug... and the perfect story to sell it.
